final_proof:
Let the two data sequences be denoted by $x^{(1)}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ and $x^{(2)}=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$, and for $i\in\{1,2\}$ let $\bar x^{(i)}=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n x_k^{(i)}$ be its mean. Put
\[
S_i=\left(\sum_{k=1}^n (x_k^{(i)}-\bar x^{(i)})^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Because $\mathbf C$ is assumed to be the (Pearson) correlation matrix of these data, its entries are defined; in particular, neither sequence has zero variance, so $S_1,S_2>0$. (If a sequence has zero variance, its Pearson correlations, and hence the stated correlation matrix, are not defined.)

For $i,j\in\{1,2\}$, the $(i,j)$-entry of $\mathbf C$ is
\[
C_{ij}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n (x_k^{(i)}-\bar x^{(i)})(x_k^{(j)}-\bar x^{(j)})}{S_iS_j}.
\]
The numerator is unchanged when $i$ and $j$ are interchanged, by commutativity of multiplication, and $S_iS_j=S_jS_i$. Therefore $C_{ij}=C_{ji}$ for every $i,j$, which proves that $\mathbf C$ is symmetric.

Taking $j=i$ gives
\[
C_{ii}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n (x_k^{(i)}-\bar x^{(i)})^2}{S_i^2}=\frac{S_i^2}{S_i^2}=1,
\]
since $S_i>0$. Thus every entry on the main diagonal of $\mathbf C$ equals $1$, as claimed. The conclusion is unchanged if sample covariances and sample standard deviations are defined using a common factor such as $1/n$ or $1/(n-1)$, because that factor cancels in the displayed ratio.
